catalog_quote: § 33. The rule for the accentuation of uncompounded words is the same in Gothic as in the oldest period of the other Germanic languages, viz. the chief stress fell upon the first syllable, and always remained there even when suffixes and inflexional endings followed it, as Audags, blessed; niman, to take; reikinon, to rule ... piudinassus, kingdom; waldufni, power. The position of the secondary stress in trisyllabic and polysyllabic words fluctuated in Gothic, and with the present state of our knowledge of the subject it is impossible to formulate any hard and fast rules concerning it. ... § 34, As has been stated above, compound words, whose second element is a noun or an adjective, had originally the chief stress on the first syllable. This simple rule was preserved in Gothic, as frakunps, OE. fracup, despised ... But in compound verbs the second element had the chief stress, as atlag…
sweep_summary: Gothic (goth1244) is in the catalog as fixed initial stress (Wright 1910 §33). The two title-works with stress in the title are both De Gruyter paywalled articles that could not be opened by any open route (DOI landing returns a bot challenge with no abstract; Unpaywall is_oa=false; Semantic Scholar/OpenAlex/CORE/archive.org/Google Scholar/academia.edu gave nothing): Suzuki 1982 (metrical approach to Gothic reduplication) is unclear/possibly stress-relevant (the stress of the reduplicating syllable is a known issue), priority medium; Pierce 2003 (Prosody and Sievers' Law) is, on the evidence of the author's companion 2006 JGL abstract and Barrack's 2010 reply (both read and saved), about syllable structure/weight, not word-stress placement, priority low. The most useful new first-hand statement obtained is the verbatim publisher abstract of Bennett 1970 'The Stress Patterns of Gothic' (PMLA), saved to primary stress fixed on word-initial syllables (roots, reduplicating syllables, prefixes incl. un-), secondary stress on second compound members, preverbs as proclitics; it confirms and refines the catalog's classification but, being abstract-only, does not supersede Wright 1910 as deciding source (full text is the high-priority acquisition, Cambridge Core/JSTOR). Streitberg 1920 §36/§231 (already held by the project, read) independently confirms initial stress with verbal compounds stressing the stem. and updated in the goth1244 our files.

new_statements.quote: In Gothic, as in Proto-Germanic, primary word stress was fixed on word-initial syllables, including roots, reduplicating syllables, and prefixes; the Gothic negative-pejorative prefix un- appears to have been no exception to the rule. Secondary word stress occurred initially on second immediate constituents of compounds and quasi-compounds; the stress of gudhŨs ‘temple’ and faurhāh ‘curtain’ was not exceptional. Weak word stress fell medially on vowels between syllables bearing other degrees of stress and on syllable-forming suffixes directly following primary or secondary stress; finally, weak word stress occurred on syllable-forming endings.
new_statements.citation: Bennett, William H. 1970. The Stress Patterns of Gothic. PMLA 85(3): 463-472. doi:10.2307/1261448
new_statements.locator: author's published abstract (Cambridge Core citation_abstract), article pp. 463-472; full text not read
new_statements.reading: Fixed primary stress on the word-initial syllable (root, reduplicating syllable, or prefix, including un-); secondary stress on the second member of compounds; weak stress on medial vowels and endings; verbal preverbs analysed as proclitics with secondary phrase stress (ga- weak), so the verb root keeps primary word stress. This is the dedicated study of Gothic stress and agrees with the catalog's 'fixed' initial coding while adding a graded stress hierarchy.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation (Wright 1910 sections 33-34, pp. 15-16) is present verbatim in the held archive.org scanned text at lines 1210-1261, under the heading 'STRESS (ACCENT)' beginning line 1142; locator matches. (2) Deciding source: a 1910 comparative reference grammar of an extinct corpus language; Gothic stress is reconstructed, not observed, and the fixed: initial syllable rule (with verbal-prefix exception) is the consensus of Germanic philology. I downloaded Streitberg 1920 Gotisches Elementarbuch (open, archive.org; whose section 36.2 (pp. 65-66) and section 231 (pp. 160-161) state the identical rule and explicitly note there is no direct testimony; Bennett 1970 PMLA (the one dedicated stress study; paywalled, abstract read on Cambridge Core) also states 'primary word stress was fixed on word-initial syllables'. (3)

sources.citation: Streitberg, Wilhelm. 1920. Gotisches Elementarbuch. 5. und 6. neubearbeitete Auflage. Heidelberg: Carl Winter.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: p. 65: 'Über die gotische Betonung sind wir durch Zeugnisse nicht unterrichtet, doch kann kein Zweifel darüber bestehn, daß auch im Gotischen das gemeingermanische Betonungsprinzip geherrscht hat, daß also der Wortakzent in heimischen Wörtern die erste Silbe getroffen haben muß. Eine Ausnahme machen nur die Verbalkomposita, die im Germanischen nicht das Präfix, sondern die Stammsilbe betonen; Näheres in § 231.' Adds (after Sievers) that compounds with monosyllabic first member, even bare particles, are stressed on the first member (gábaurþai, gáqumþim), un- compounds have double main stress. S
sources.locator: section 36 Anhang '2. Betonung', pp. 65-66 (the scanned text); section 231 'Akzentuierung der Komposita', pp. 160-161 (the scanned text)
sources.note: §36 Anhang '2. Betonung' (pp. 65-66; the scanned text): no direct testimony for Gothic accent, but no doubt that the Common Germanic principle held, i.e. the word accent in native words fell on the first syllable; the only exception is verbal compounds, which stress the stem syllable, not the prefix (§231). Nominal compounds with monosyllabic first member show the pattern stressed-unstressed-stressed (gabaurþai, gaqumþai); compounds with un- have double main stress. §231 (pp. 160-161, the scanned text): Germanic nominal compounds accent the first member, verbal compounds the second; this rule…
